title: ChatGPT, Claude & Gemini with Excel
goal: Prepare a safe copy of a sheet for a chatbot, then turn its answers back into formulas you own, adapted to your own columns.

steps.topic: An answer in chat is not in your sheet
steps.text:
ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini can all take a spreadsheet and answer questions about it. The routine is the same for each:

• **Prepare** a safe copy
• **Upload** it and ask
• **Check** the answer
• **Bring it back** as a formula you own

Tools and plans differ in what they can do with a file. Some run calculations on it; others only read it as text and may miss rows in a long file. So check, always.

Here's why step 4 matters. Press the button: the number pasted from chat stays put, while the formula follows your data.

steps.prompt:
You want a chatbot to total sales by region. It needs only **Region** and **Amount**.

Select those two columns, headers included: drag from ==B1== to ==C5==, then press [[Enter]].
steps.wrongFeedback: Select just the Region and Amount columns, from `B1` (the header) down to `C5`. Leave out the names and phone numbers.
clues: Start on B1, the word Region, and drag to the last amount in column C.

steps.topic: Paste values into a fresh file
steps.prompt:
You've copied `B1:C5` and opened a **new, empty workbook**. Paste **values only**: that leaves behind formulas, hidden sheets, comments and links from the original.

Press [[Ctrl]] + [[Alt]] + [[V]], then [[V]] for **Values**, then [[Enter]].
clues: Ctrl + Alt + V together, then V alone, then Enter. On a Mac, use the Paste Special menu and choose Values.

steps.prompt: Before uploading, which is the **safest** way to prepare the file for a chatbot?
options: Upload the original: the chatbot will ignore the private columns
Upload a copy with only the columns it needs, IDs instead of names, and no hidden sheets
Hide the private columns, then upload the original
steps.explain: A small, clean copy means nothing private can leak. Also check your workplace policy and the tool's data settings first: some plans may use what you upload to improve their models, others don't.
wrongFeedback: The chatbot can read every column in the file, whether or not you mention it.
Hidden columns are still inside the file. Delete them from a copy instead.
clues: Which option removes the private data instead of just covering it?

steps.prompt:
A chatbot replies: “Pune's total is **8,400**.” You copy that number into `E2`. A week later you add another Pune order to your sheet.

What does `E2` show?
options: Still `8,400`: it's just a typed number
steps.explain: A number pasted from a chat is just typed text, with no link to your cells. That's why you ask the chatbot for the **formula** too, and paste that instead.
wrongFeedback: Only a formula updates. A pasted number has nothing connected to your data.
Nothing is broken; the number simply never moves. That's the problem.
clues: Did you paste a formula or a number?

steps.prompt: The chatbot said Pune's total is **8,400**. Now make it yours: in ==D2== write a formula that works out Pune's total from your data.
steps.explain: **8400**, matching the chatbot, and it now moves with your data. Reproducing a chatbot's answer with your own formula is also the best check that it was right.

wrongFeedback.missingFunction: Add up the amounts for one region: `SUMIF`.
wrongFeedback.wrongValue: Add only Pune's rows (3500 and 4900) to get 8400.

steps.prompt:
A chatbot guessed your layout and gave `=SUMIFS(C:C,B:B,"Pune",A:A,"Q2")`. But in **your** sheet the amounts are in column B and the regions in column C.

Rewrite it in ==E2== to match your columns.
steps.explain: **1200** (500 + 700). A chatbot can't see your sheet's real layout, so its formula often points at the wrong columns. Read each range and ask: is this where my amounts, regions and quarters really are?

wrongFeedback.missingFunction: You need two conditions on one total: `SUMIFS`, with the amount range first.
wrongFeedback.wrongValue: Amounts are in `B`, regions in `C`, quarters in `A`. Only Pune **and** Q2 rows count: 500 + 700.

steps.prompt:
A chatbot gave `=LET(t,SUM(B2:B7),n,COUNT(B2:B7),t/n)` for the average order. You'd rather have a version you can read at a glance.

Write the plain version in ==D2==, with no `LET`.
steps.explain: **50.** `LET` only gives names to the pieces (`t` the total, `n` the count), and `t/n` is an average. If you can't rewrite a chatbot's formula in your own words, you don't own it yet. Either ask it to explain, or ask for a simpler version.

wrongFeedback.wrongValue: The average of the six amounts is 50. Total ÷ count, or `AVERAGE`.

steps.topic: A function your Excel doesn't have
steps.prompt: The chatbot gave you a formula starting `=GROUPBY(`, and your Excel shows `#NAME?`. What's the **best next move**?
options: Tell it which Excel you have and ask for a `SUMIFS` version
Retype the formula in capital letters
steps.explain: Newer functions such as `GROUPBY` or `LET` aren't in every Excel, and older versions lack even `XLOOKUP`. Tell the chatbot your version (“Excel 2019”) and ask for an alternative made from functions you have, like `SUMIFS`.
wrongFeedback: Capitals make no difference: Excel doesn't care. It simply doesn't know the function.
The same formula gives the same `#NAME?`. Something has to change: the function.
clues: `#NAME?` means Excel doesn't recognise a name. What can you ask for instead?

steps.prompt: In chat, the AI listed your regions as Pune, Goa, Delhi. Own that list: starting in ==D2== write a formula that lists each region in `A2:A7` **once**.
steps.explain: **Pune, Goa, Delhi** spill down from `D2`. Add a new region to the data and the list grows, which a list typed from the chat never will.

wrongFeedback.wrongValue: You want each region once, in order of first appearance, filling downwards from `D2`.

clues: One function removes the repeats from a range.

steps.prompt: A chatbot says: “The average of the orders **over 1,000** is **1,750**.” Own it. In ==D2== write a formula that produces that number from your data, not a typed number.
steps.explain: **1750** (1500, 2000 and 1750). The order of exactly 1000 isn't “over”, so it stays out: with `>=` you'd get 1562.5. Matching the chatbot's number with your own formula is proof that it was right.

wrongFeedback.wrongValue: Average only the orders **over** 1,000 (not equal to 1,000): 1500, 2000 and 1750.

clues: Average only the amounts greater than 1000.
